challenges.name: validate-model-output
challenges.title: Validating a model's score
challenges.description: Two statements about the grading service after the gradebook was corrupted by model replies: one about a one-line "repair" of the score, one about capping the AI score with the automated tests.

questions.explanation: False. Number("10/10") and Number(undefined) are NaN, and Math.round, Math.max and Math.min all return NaN for NaN, so two of these replies still write NaN (PostgreSQL's numeric type even accepts 'NaN'). The other two are worse because they look fine: 11 silently becomes 10, and -1 - the model's way of saying it could not grade - becomes 0, a failing grade the learner did not earn. Clamping turns an invalid reply into a valid-looking one and erases the evidence. Reject the reply, keep the AI score empty, send the submission to human review with the reason, and record the decision. The misconception is that coercing a value into range is the same as validating it.

questions.question:
Grading policy (v2): an AI score is accepted only if it is an integer 0-10 and at most the automated test score + 2; otherwise the submission goes to human review.

Decision log:
submission  tests  model reply                                  decision
sub_91c2    3/10   {"score": 9, "feedback": "Perfect solution."}  review (above_test_cap)
sub_91c3    7/10   {"score": 8, "feedback": "Clear names, ..."}    accepted

Statement: "Under this policy, a prompt injection that makes the model return 10 on a submission passing 3 of 10 tests can no longer put more than 5 in the gradebook: the reply goes to a human instead."
questions.explanation: True. The cap ties the AI score to evidence the learner cannot talk to: the automated tests. With 3 of 10 tests, the highest AI score that is accepted is 5, and any higher reply - a 9 as in sub_91c2, or the injected 10 from lesson 3.1 - is not written but routed to review with the reason above_test_cap. The cap does not detect the injection; it limits what a successful one is worth, and the review queue turns it into a signal. The decision log is what lets you prove this later. The misconception is that output validation is only about the format of the reply.

challenges.name: validate-model-output
challenges.title: Fix It: a Model Score Written Straight to the Database
challenges.description: The CodeDev grading service asks the AI grader for JSON { "score": <integer 0-10>, "feedback": "<text>" } and handleGradingResult writes the reply straight into the gradebook (UPDATE submissions SET ai_score = output.score). Since the new grading prompt went live the gradebook shows scores of 11, -1 and 9.5, submissions that stay without a score, and grading jobs that fail with invalid input syntax for type numeric: "10/10" until they are dead-lettered. Fix handleGradingResult so that a reply is never repaired: it is accepted only when it is a JSON object whose score is an integer from 0 to 10, whose feedback is a string of 10 to 1000 characters after trimming, and whose score is at most the automated test score + 2. An accepted reply is written with db.updateAiScore(id, score, feedback). Any other reply leaves the AI score empty and goes to human review with db.sendToReview(id, reason), where reason is the first failed check, in this order: invalid_json (not JSON, or not a JSON object), score_missing (absent or null), score_not_integer (not a JSON number, or not an integer), score_out_of_range, feedback_missing (not a string), feedback_length, above_test_cap. Every job records exactly one decision with db.recordDecision({ submissionId, outcome: "accepted" | "review", reason }) (reason null when accepted). Do not change the database fake or the test runner. Input: { jobs: [{ submissionId, testScore, modelOutput }] }. Output: the gradebook, the review queue, the decisions and the jobs that threw. The public tests include the replies from the incident; the hidden tests cover decimals, strings, non-JSON replies, feedback limits, the test cap and a large recorded batch.
hints: What does the database do with a value that is not a valid score? Run the starter on the incident test and compare the gradebook with the failures: which bad replies crash the job, and which ones are quietly stored?

Everything happens in handleGradingResult: JSON.parse can throw, output.score can be any JSON value, and updateAiScore is called before anything is checked. Look at the order of the checks in the header comment: write one function that returns the first failed reason or null, and only call updateAiScore when it returns null.

A similar case on different data: a reply for a difficulty estimate must be { "level": integer 1-5 }. {"level": "3"} fails as level_not_integer (a string is not a JSON number), {"level": 4.5} fails the same way, {"level": 6} fails as level_out_of_range, and none of them is rounded or clamped: each goes to review with its reason and a decision is recorded, while {"level": 3} is written as 3.
